title: Fixing an outdated setup guide
question: On your second day you follow the team's setup guide and find three steps that are wrong or missing. You get everything running after a few hours of trial and error. What is the best thing to do next?
options: Keep the fixes in your personal notes, because editing the shared guide as a newcomer may look like criticism of the team
Update the guide with the corrections you found, so the next person to join does not hit the same gaps
Post a long message in the team channel listing everything that is wrong with the guide and ask someone else to rewrite it
Wait until your probation period is over before touching the guide, in case the gaps were caused by your own mistakes
explanation: A new joiner is the only person who sees the setup with fresh eyes, so updating the guide (or opening a small change for it) is one of the most useful early contributions. Private notes help only you, a complaint without a fix creates work for others and the guide stays wrong, and waiting for the end of probation means several more people lose hours on the same gaps.

title: Choosing a first ticket
question: Your manager lets you pick your first ticket from the backlog. Which one is the best choice for a first week?
options: The cross-service migration nobody wants, because taking the hardest work early shows ambition and earns trust quickly
The ticket with the vaguest description, because working without guidance shows autonomy and saves your teammates' time
A redesign of the core module, because touching the most important code is the fastest way to learn how everything fits
A small bug in a single module, with clear acceptance criteria and a teammate who knows the area
explanation: A first ticket should be small, low risk and well defined, so you can complete the whole path (branch, tests, review, deploy) and learn the team's process with a quick win. A migration, a vague ticket or a core redesign mixes too many unknowns: you cannot tell whether a problem comes from the code, the process or the requirements, and a stalled first task hurts confidence.

title: Where local API keys belong
question: The project needs an API key for a staging service to run on your machine. A teammate says everyone just pastes it into a config file in the repository. Where should the key live?
options: In a git-ignored local file or the team's secret manager, never committed to the repository
In the committed config file, since the repository is private and only people at the company can read it
In a committed file, but encoded in Base64 so that it is not readable at a glance by anyone browsing the code
In your personal cloud notes, pasted back into the committed config whenever you need to run the project
explanation: Secrets committed to a repository stay in its history, get copied into clones and forks, and are hard to revoke later, even when the repository is private. Keep them in untracked local files or a secret manager and rotate any key that was exposed. Base64 is an encoding rather than protection, and pasting from notes into a committed file still ends with the key in the history.

title: Your first 1:1 with your manager
question: You have your first 1:1 with your manager in week one. Which approach sets you up best for the next three months?
options: Avoid talking about goals until you have settled in, and use the time to ask for a long list of tasks so you always look busy
Ask which results would justify a raise or a promotion, and by when, so your effort goes into the right things from the start
Ask what success looks like at 30, 60 and 90 days, and how they prefer to give feedback and receive updates
Keep the meeting purely social, because goals and feedback are the manager's job and will be brought up when they are ready
explanation: Agreeing early on what good looks like at 30, 60 and 90 days, and how you will get feedback, removes guesswork and avoids surprises at review time. Asking for a pile of tasks measures activity instead of outcomes, opening with raise timelines is premature before you have delivered anything, and a purely social meeting wastes the best moment to align expectations.

title: Learning the team's working agreements
question: After a week you notice the team has habits you were never told about, such as when to update tickets and how fast to answer chat messages. What is the best way to learn them?
options: Apply the conventions from your previous company, since they are common industry practice and the team will adapt to you
Wait until someone corrects you, because mistakes are the clearest signal of what the team really expects from newcomers
Ask each teammate individually to describe their personal rules and follow whichever approach the majority prefers
Look for written working agreements, observe how the team behaves, and ask a teammate about anything undocumented
explanation: Working agreements (ticket hygiene, response times, meeting norms) are often partly written and partly implicit, so combining the written material with observation and a few targeted questions gets you aligned fastest. Importing old habits can clash with local norms, learning only through corrections is slow and stressful, and polling everyone one by one costs time and still misses what the team agreed together.

title: Too many meetings and acronyms
question: In your first two weeks you attend many meetings full of acronyms, system names and decisions that reference earlier discussions. By Friday you are mixing things up. What is the most effective habit to build?
options: Keep a running glossary plus a log of decisions and open questions, then bring the open ones to a teammate in a batch
Ask the speaker to define every acronym on the spot, even if it interrupts the discussion, so nothing is left unclear
Record every meeting and rewatch the recordings on weekends, so no detail is lost while you absorb the whole context
Rely on memory for now and ask only when an item directly blocks a task, since most terms become obvious with time
explanation: A living glossary and decision log turns scattered information into something you can search, and batching the open questions respects other people's focus while still closing your gaps quickly. Interrupting for each term derails the meeting, rewatching recordings is a heavy time cost with little structure, and relying on memory leaves you guessing until a term blocks real work.

title: Learning an unfamiliar business domain
question: You joined a company that builds software for clinic scheduling, a domain you know nothing about. Tickets mention terms like no-show, overbooking and referral. How should you build domain knowledge?
options: Focus only on the code for now, since the domain rules are all encoded there and will become clear as you read it
Read a book about clinic management cover to cover before taking any ticket, so you never build something based on guesses
Use the product as a customer would and shadow support or operations, tying each ticket to the user problem it solves
Ask the product manager to explain every ticket in detail before you start, so the business context never has to be guessed
explanation: Seeing real users and their problems (by using the product, sitting in on support calls or watching operations) gives you the context that code and tickets omit, and linking each ticket to its user problem improves your decisions. Code shows what the system does but not why, a full book delays all contribution, and depending on one person for every explanation does not scale.

title: Meeting people beyond your team
question: In week two your manager suggests you meet people outside your immediate team, but everyone looks busy and you feel you would be intruding. What is the most effective approach?
options: Wait for them to approach you, since people who are busy will reach out once they have something concrete to discuss
Book short intro chats with product, QA, design and support, asking about their work and what they need from engineering
Meet only the most senior engineers on your team, because they can help your career more than anyone in other roles
Postpone the meetings until you have shipped your first feature, so you have something worth talking about when you meet
explanation: Short, prepared conversations with neighbouring roles reveal how your work reaches users, who to ask for what, and what those roles need from you, and they build relationships before you urgently need them. Waiting passively delays that map, focusing only on seniors skips the people your work depends on, and holding off until a first feature ships means you work for weeks without that context.

title: Where to start in a large codebase
question: You are handed a repository with hundreds of files and no architecture document. What is the most effective way to start understanding it?
options: Pick one user-visible flow and follow it from its entry point, such as a route or handler, down through each layer
Read every file in alphabetical order from the top folder, so that no part of the system is skipped along the way
Start with the shared utilities folder, because those helpers are used everywhere and explain the building blocks first
Open the largest file in the project first, because the biggest file usually holds the core business logic
explanation: Following a single concrete flow gives you a path through the layers with a clear purpose, and each new flow adds to a mental map. Reading alphabetically has no connection to how the code runs, utilities make little sense before you know their callers, and file size says more about accumulated history than about importance.

title: Seeing how data moves through the code
question: You cannot tell from reading alone how a request ends up calling a particular function deep in the code. What is the quickest way to find out?
options: Keep reading the source until the path becomes clear, since running the app might change its behaviour and mislead you
Add log statements to every layer and keep them in the codebase afterwards so that the next newcomer can follow the same trail
Run the app locally, set a breakpoint in that function, trigger the request and inspect the call stack
Ask the original author to explain the whole module, and avoid touching anything until you have heard the full story
explanation: A breakpoint shows the real path: the call stack lists every caller, and you can inspect the actual values at each step. Reading alone cannot resolve dynamic dispatch, configuration or dependency injection, permanent logs in every layer add noise for everyone, and asking for a full explanation costs another person's time when the debugger answers a narrow question in minutes.

title: Learning intended behaviour from tests
question: You need to change a function that has no comments or documentation. Where can you most reliably learn its intended behaviour and edge cases?
options: In the function's name, because a well-chosen name already describes every case the code handles
In its existing tests, which show example inputs, expected outputs and the edge cases the team cared about
In the deployment configuration, because it shows which inputs the function receives when it runs in production
In the repository's top-level README, because it documents the contract of each function in the project
explanation: Tests are executable examples: they state expected results for concrete inputs and often capture edge cases and past bugs, and they fail if they drift from the code. A name is a hint and not a full contract, deployment settings do not describe function behaviour, and a README rarely covers individual functions.

title: A strange condition nobody explains
question: While reading a function you find a strange `if` that special-cases one customer id, with no comment. What should you do first to understand why it exists?
options: Delete the condition on your branch and see what breaks, since an unexplained special case is probably a leftover
Assume it was a mistake and leave a comment saying it is dead code, so that someone else decides what to do with it
Raise it in the next team meeting without looking at the history, so the whole team can speculate about its origin
Use git blame or log on that line to find the commit and its linked ticket or pull request, which usually explain the reason
explanation: History is the cheapest source of context: git blame points to the commit, and the message, ticket or pull request often explains the business reason. Deleting it risks reintroducing the very problem it fixed, calling it dead code without evidence spreads a guess, and starting a group discussion before checking the history spends several people's time on something one command can answer.

title: Finding every caller of a function
question: You must change the signature of a function and need to know everywhere it is used. What is the most reliable first step?
options: Open the files in the same folder one by one, since callers are almost always located next to the function itself
Ask teammates to list the callers from memory, because they know the code better than any search tool does
Use the IDE's find usages feature, and back it up with a text search over the repository for dynamic or string references
Read the module's documentation page, since it lists every internal and external caller of each function
explanation: Find usages uses the code's structure to list real references, and a text search catches what static analysis can miss, such as reflection, configuration files or strings. Callers are often far from the function, memory is incomplete in a large codebase, and documentation pages go stale and rarely list callers at all.

title: Messy code and the urge to rewrite
question: You are fixing a small bug in a tangled 600-line class and badly want to rewrite it. You have been on the team for three weeks and the class has few tests. What is the best approach?
options: Rewrite the class first so you can understand it while cleaning, and fix the bug afterwards in the tidier structure
Make the minimal fix, add tests that pin current behaviour, and propose the refactor separately once you understand the code
Leave the class exactly as it is and mention nothing, because newcomers should not question existing design decisions
Do the cleanup in the same change as the fix, so the codebase is left in better shape than you found it
explanation: Messy code often carries hidden behaviour and past bug fixes that you cannot see yet, so a minimal fix with tests that pin current behaviour keeps risk low, and a separate, informed refactor proposal lets the team weigh in. Rewriting first risks breaking behaviour you misread, staying silent wastes useful observations, and mixing cleanup into the fix makes both harder to verify and to roll back.

title: Keeping your bearings in the system
question: Two weeks in, you still get lost when a ticket crosses several modules and services. What habit best builds a lasting understanding of the system?
options: Study the directory tree every morning until you have memorised where each folder and file lives
Wait until you feel comfortable on your own, since understanding builds up naturally as tickets accumulate
Generate a diagram of every class with a tool and read it, so that you have a complete picture of the codebase at once
Sketch a simple map of modules, data stores and external calls as you trace flows, and share it to be corrected
explanation: Drawing the map as you trace real flows forces you to decide what matters, and sharing it exposes wrong assumptions early while giving the team a reusable artifact. Memorising folders captures layout but not behaviour, passive waiting is slow and uneven, and an auto-generated diagram of every class is too dense to reveal how the important flows actually work.

title: Requesting a guided tour of a subsystem
question: After three days of reading the billing module you understand the main flow, but several parts remain unclear. The original author is on your team and busy. What is the best way to close the gaps?
options: Ask for a 30-minute walkthrough, bringing your sketch of the flow and a short list of specific questions
Ask them to explain the whole billing system from scratch, so that you do not build on partial or incorrect assumptions
Keep reading until you have covered every file, since asking too early shows that you did not do your homework
Message them for links to existing documentation and do nothing more, so that you never take up their time
explanation: A short walkthrough that starts from your own sketch and specific questions makes the best use of the author's time, because they only need to confirm and fill in what you already built. Asking for everything from scratch ignores your progress and takes far longer, reading everything first delays you past the point of diminishing returns, and asking only for links skips the context that documents rarely hold.

title: Time-boxing before you ask
question: You are new, stuck on a problem, and unsure when asking becomes the right call. Which rule of thumb works best?
options: Never ask until you have solved the problem yourself, because struggling alone proves independence and earns respect
Set a time box of 30 to 60 minutes, try on your own, then ask even if unfinished, shortening it when work is urgent
Ask at the first sign of difficulty, so that you never lose any time and teammates always see how engaged you are
Keep trying until the end of the day and then ask, since asking mid-day always interrupts someone's deep focus
explanation: A time box balances learning from the struggle against the cost of being blocked: you build your own debugging skills but do not burn hours on something a teammate could unblock in minutes, and urgency can shorten it. Never asking hides problems and wastes days, asking immediately skips the learning and produces vague questions, and waiting until evening is an arbitrary rule that ignores how much is at stake.

title: What a good question contains
question: Your local build fails after pulling the latest changes, and you want a teammate to help quickly. Which message is most likely to get a fast, useful answer?
options: A screenshot of your IDE with the message "the build is broken again, any idea what is happening?"
The full 2,000-line build log pasted into the chat, with the note "the error is somewhere in there, please take a look"
A detailed chronological story of everything you did on the project this week, including the last three tickets you worked on
The goal, the exact error text, what you already tried and what you expected to happen instead
explanation: A good question lets the other person start helping without a round of clarifications: the goal, the exact error text, what you tried and the gap between expected and actual behaviour. A vague screenshot forces them to interrogate you, a raw log dump moves the diagnosis work onto them, and a long chronology buries the relevant detail among irrelevant events.

title: Reducing a bug before asking
question: A bug shows up only in a checkout flow that touches many services, and after an hour you cannot find the cause. Before you ask a teammate, what step makes your question easiest to answer?
options: Shrink it to the smallest steps, input or failing test that still shows the problem, and share exactly that
Give the teammate access to your branch and the full running app, and ask them to find the problem the way you did
Write a prose description of the whole architecture of the checkout flow, so they have the complete context first
Wait until they are free to pair, then reproduce the full flow live so they can watch every service involved
explanation: Reducing a problem to a minimal reproduction often reveals the cause on its own, and when it does not, it gives the helper a small, concrete thing to examine instead of the whole system. Handing over the full app repeats your hour of work for them, an architecture essay does not show where the failure is, and reproducing the full flow live burns the shared time you want to use efficiently.

title: Public channel or direct message
question: You do not understand how the deployment pipeline picks the target environment, and several people on the team probably could answer. Where should you ask?
options: In a direct message to the most senior engineer, since they will give the fastest and most accurate answer
In direct messages to a few teammates one by one, so that no single person feels responsible for answering
In the team's public channel, so the answer is searchable and others with the same doubt benefit
In the next all-hands meeting, where the whole company can weigh in and the answer reaches the most people
explanation: A question in a shared channel gets answers from whoever is free, leaves a searchable record and lets others learn from it. A direct message to one senior person makes them a bottleneck and the answer stays private, messaging several people separately duplicates effort and creates conflicting answers, and an all-hands is the wrong venue for a routine technical question.

title: After getting an answer
question: A teammate spends 20 minutes explaining why failed payments are retried in a particular way. It is not written anywhere. What is the best follow-up?
options: Keep it in your private notes, because they are organised the way you think and nobody else needs them
Trust your memory, since a concept that was explained once by the person who built it will stay with you
Ask the teammate to write it up themselves, because they know the details and should own the documentation
Write the explanation into the team's docs, ask the teammate to check it, and link it in the channel
explanation: Writing the answer down turns a one-off conversation into lasting knowledge, and having the teammate review it catches misunderstandings while the explanation is fresh. Private notes help only you, memory fades quickly for details you rarely use, and handing the writing back to the busiest expert delays it and wastes the effort you are best placed to do.

title: A chat thread that keeps growing
question: You have been trading messages with a teammate for 40 minutes about a configuration problem, and each answer raises two new questions. What is the best next move?
options: Suggest a short call or pairing session with screen sharing, and summarise the outcome in the thread afterwards
Keep going in chat but write much longer messages, so each one covers every possible follow-up question in advance
Pause the conversation until the afternoon, hoping that distance from the problem helps both of you see it more clearly
Thank them and keep investigating alone, since 40 minutes of their time is already more than a newcomer should use
explanation: When each reply spawns new questions, text is the slow channel: a short call with a shared screen lets the helper see your actual setup and correct you in real time, and a summary afterwards preserves the result. Longer messages cannot anticipate unknown follow-ups, pausing leaves you blocked, and stopping because you fear taking too much time often costs more total time for both of you.

title: Blocked two days before the sprint ends
question: The sprint ends on Friday. On Wednesday you realise you have been stuck on a third-party integration for a day and a half and will not finish in time. What is the best action?
options: Work evenings and the weekend to catch up quietly, so the team sees the work delivered and never hears about the delay
Ship a partial version behind a flag on Friday without mentioning the gaps, and finish the rest during next sprint
Tell your lead now, with a short status, what is blocking you and options such as asking for help, reducing scope or moving the date
Ask a teammate to take over the ticket without explaining why, so that the sprint goal is still met by someone else
explanation: Early, specific communication gives the team time to adjust: they can unblock you, cut scope or replan, while a late surprise offers no options. Hidden overtime is unsustainable and hides a real estimation or process problem, shipping gaps silently creates risk for people who rely on the feature, and passing the ticket on without context wastes what you learned and the handover opportunity.

title: Asking again without feeling like a burden
question: You asked a teammate the same kind of question twice this week and you now fear being seen as a burden. How do you keep learning quickly without wearing out your teammates?
options: Stop asking questions and rely on trial and error until you feel confident, so that nobody has to spend time on you
Keep notes of past answers, bring your own hypothesis to each question, and keep asking about truly new things
Save all questions for a weekly meeting, even blocking ones, so interruptions stay low and everyone's focus is protected
Ask a different teammate each time, so that no single person is asked often enough to feel that you are leaning on them
explanation: Notes prevent repeated questions, and a hypothesis ("I think it works like X because of Y, right?") shows effort, speeds up the answer and exposes wrong mental models, while continuing to ask about new things keeps your learning curve steep. Silence turns small blockers into days of lost time, a weekly batch leaves you blocked in between, and rotating helpers only hides the pattern without fixing the cause.

title: Hearing critical feedback calmly
question: In a 1:1, your manager says your last three tickets were delivered without tests. What is the most constructive response?
options: Listen, ask for a concrete example or two, thank them and agree on what you will do differently next time
Explain at length why each ticket was rushed, so your manager understands the circumstances before judging the result
Agree immediately and say nothing more, to show that you accept the feedback without any resistance whatsoever
Ask for the feedback to be put in writing first, so that you can check whether the examples are really fair and accurate
explanation: Listening, clarifying with examples and committing to a specific change shows that you take feedback seriously and turns it into progress. Long explanations sound defensive and bury the point, silent agreement leaves you unclear about what to change, and asking for a written record first treats feedback as an accusation instead of a chance to improve.

title: Seeking feedback during probation
question: You are six weeks into a three-month probation period and have received almost no feedback. You feel unsure about how you are doing. What is the best step?
options: Assume that silence means things are going well, and avoid raising the topic so as not to look insecure
Ask the whole team in the group channel how you are doing, and treat the average of the replies as your evaluation
Ask your manager for specific feedback, such as the one change that would help most, and agree on check-ins
Wait for the formal probation review, since that is the official moment when feedback is meant to be given
explanation: Asking for specific, forward-looking feedback early gives you time to adjust and shows initiative, and agreeing on check-ins makes expectations visible before any formal review. Silence is not a signal, public polling produces polite and vague answers that do not reflect your manager's view, and waiting for the formal review means any problem is revealed when it is too late to fix.

title: Making the most of your 1:1
question: Your weekly 1:1 with your manager often turns into a ticket status review, and you leave without having discussed what worries you. How should you change it?
options: Let your manager drive the conversation, since they know best which topics matter and will raise whatever is important
Prepare a short agenda of blockers, questions and growth topics, and keep status updates out of the meeting
Use the time to walk through every open ticket in detail, so your manager always has an up-to-date view of your work
Skip the 1:1 in weeks when nothing is going wrong, to avoid wasting your manager's time on routine conversations
explanation: A 1:1 exists for you as much as for your manager, so an agenda with blockers, questions and growth topics makes the time useful, and status is better handled in tickets or standups. Waiting for your manager to steer means your concerns never come up, a ticket walkthrough duplicates information elsewhere, and skipping the meeting removes the regular channel where small issues are cheapest to solve.

title: Shaping a realistic growth plan
question: Your manager asks you to propose a growth plan for the next six months. Which proposal is most likely to produce real progress?
options: A long list of technologies to learn this year, so that every area of the stack is covered and nobody can say you have gaps
A copy of a senior engineer's career path, since it has already proven to lead to promotion on this team
No plan for now, because it is more realistic to wait for the end of probation and see what the company needs from you
Two or three concrete goals with observable outcomes and checkpoints, agreed with your manager and reviewed in your 1:1s
explanation: A few specific goals with outcomes you can observe (for example, own a small feature end to end, or lead a debugging session) are easier to track and make your manager a partner in reaching them. A long list of technologies spreads effort thin and measures exposure instead of impact, copying another person's path ignores your strengths and interests, and postponing the plan leaves growth to chance.

title: You broke production
question: You ran a data migration that locked a table and made checkout fail for ten minutes before it was rolled back. People are asking what happened. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Quietly roll everything back and say nothing, since the problem is already fixed and drawing attention to it helps nobody
Take time first to write a perfect root-cause analysis, and only tell the team once you can explain every detail of it
Say right away what you ran and when, help restore service, and then contribute a factual timeline to the blameless postmortem
Step away from the incident and let senior engineers handle it, so that you cannot make the situation any worse
explanation: Fast, honest information is what responders need most, and a blameless postmortem focuses on the factors that let the change cause harm, such as missing safeguards or review, instead of on the person. Hiding the event removes the learning and the chance to prevent a repeat, delaying disclosure prolongs the outage, and withdrawing removes the person who knows the most about what was run.

title: Work that nobody notices
question: You spent two weeks fixing a flaky test suite, cutting average build time from 25 to 12 minutes. Nobody has mentioned it. What is the best way to make this work visible?
options: Let the merged commits speak for themselves, since good work is eventually noticed by everyone who benefits from it
Post a short update in the team channel with the before and after numbers, and mention it in your next 1:1
Announce it in the company-wide channel with a celebratory message, so that leadership knows exactly who did it
Ask your manager to announce it on your behalf at the next meeting, since the news will carry more weight coming from them
explanation: A brief update with concrete numbers is factual, shows the impact and gives your manager material for your review without exaggerating. Commits rarely tell the story of impact, a company-wide celebration is out of proportion for a team-level improvement and can seem self-promotional, and delegating the announcement relies on your manager remembering the details.

title: A deadline that does not fit the estimate
question: A product manager asks you to deliver a feature by Friday. You estimate two weeks, but as a junior you feel you should say yes. What is the best response?
options: Say yes and work late to make it, since proving yourself early matters more than protecting your schedule
Say no right away because the estimate is two weeks, and explain that the date is simply not possible for you
Say yes and trim the tests and edge cases to hit the date, planning to add them in a later cleanup sprint
Share your estimate and its drivers, and offer options such as a smaller slice by Friday, involving your lead
explanation: Sharing your estimate with its reasoning and proposing alternatives, such as cutting scope or phasing delivery, treats the date as a negotiation about outcomes rather than a verdict. Agreeing and burning out, or cutting tests, only moves the cost to later with more risk, and a flat no without options leaves the product manager nothing to work with.

title: Impostor feelings and long hours
question: In month four you work late most nights, feel like you do not belong, and have started avoiding questions so nobody sees what you do not know. What is the best course of action?
options: Talk openly with your manager or a mentor about workload and doubts, and agree on realistic priorities and support
Work even more hours until the feeling goes away, because competence will eventually catch up with the effort you put in
Keep it to yourself until the probation review is over, so that nobody questions whether you are the right fit for the job
Switch to a lighter task list on your own and stop volunteering, so you can recover without having to explain anything
explanation: Impostor feelings and overwork reinforce each other, and they are common among people early in a career. Naming them to a manager or mentor lets someone check your calibration, adjust workload and offer support, which is far more effective than silence. More hours drive burnout without fixing the doubt, hiding it until probation ends lets it grow, and quietly reducing your scope can look like disengagement.
